pr_title: Rest api to reset deprecation indexing cache
pr_body:
Deprecation indexing is using RateLimitingFilter to throttle duplicated
deprecations. 
This commit adds REST API and transport actions to reset the LRU cache in this filter.

This will not affect the log4j filter used for throttling file appenders.
usage is very simple. Just call `DELETE` on `_logging/deprecation_cache`
```
curl --request DELETE \
  --url http://localhost:9200/_logging/deprecation_cache \
  --header 'Authorization: Basic ZWxhc3RpYzpwYXNzd29yZA=='
```
closes #78134
pr_comments: Since resetting the cache is not deprecated, I don’t think it should be logged as such. You could log as debug?

we can log as debug. But this would mean that the log line will be in server log files only. It would not appear in deprecation data stream.
I agree that logging as warn deprecation might be confusing (I wanted to avoid this by introducing a new category). 
but then again, maybe I am overdoing this and we don't need that information in deprecation data stream at all.

@cjcenizal do you know how the Upgrade Assitant UI is planning to use this API and then present fresh deprecations? Is the "marker" indicating a reset being performed needed at all?

@pgomulka We expect the following workflow:

1. Users will enable deprecation logging
2. As applications send requests using deprecated API features, they'll see a log counter increase
3. They'll review the logs in an analysis UI, such as Discover, to identify the requests at fault
4. They'll fix and redeploy an application (or all of them)
5. They'll reset the counter, and wait for the count to go back up
6. If it goes up, they'll continue the process at step 3, and if it doesn't go up then they'll have confidence their fixes were effective

Does this make sense?
BTW you can test this out yourself by spinning up a fresh 7.16 deployment on Cloud.

The word "counter" makes me worry here - we use a rate limiting mechanism so that we don't keep logging the same message over and over, which means counting the occurrences of each message could be wildly inaccurate.

@pugnascotia I think it all depends on how we present it to the user. For example, we could present it as "a count of unique logs". But I think you and anyone else should try out the UX and see how it feels.

so there is a counter. I suspect it counts how many documents are there in deprecation log data stream As @pugnascotia mentioned reseting the indexing cache means that deprecations that already were indexed can be indexed again (duplicated). In step 5: > They'll reset the counter, and wait for the count to go back up I feel that by reseting the counter you mean removing the documents from deprecation log index? Data streams are append only, so I think it is not possible. The count on the UI would not go down, unless you remember what was the previous count. With a marker we could query for the last `reset cache`. Take the timestamp. And then query for documents with timestamp greater then the fetched latest `reset cache`

This is the deprecation log counter. It's just below the UI in your screenshot.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1238659/135283250-b50521ee-7e58-446b-9c6b-429569bf78ee.png)

> I feel that by reseting the counter you mean removing the documents from deprecation log index?

No. The way we've implemented this counter is we store a timestamp when the user clicks "Reset counter" and count all new docs that have been indexed since that timestamp.

so that solves it all :) I will remove the redundant log indicating a reset 
thanks @cjcenizal !

@cjcenizal good question. I am not sure if this should be treated more like internal API or we should publicly document this. I don't mind either approach.

issue_context.title: Expose ability to invalidate deprecation log cache
issue_context.body:
Elasticsearch maintains an internal cache to represent each unique deprecation message. This helps to prevent spamming the deprecation logs with too much identical information. As a result, a deprecation message is only emitted to the log the first time it is encountered after a fresh start. Normally this is desirable. 

However, recently the Kibana Upgrade Assistant introduced a friendly UI to expose these deprecation logs inside Kibana. As part of the workflow, the user can "reset" the last time they reviewed the deprecation logs. This is to help a user remember the last time they examined the logs. The workflow is a user will read the logs, fix the deprecation, hit "reset", and then after a while has passed review any new log messages since the last "reset". Unless the user also restarts the servers, it will not reset the ability to for Elasticsearch to emit the deprecation logs. 

This request is to expose an API that Kibana can call when the user clicks the "reset" button that will invalidate the cache of emitted deprecation logs. This will allow a user to click "reset" in the Kibana UI and then deprecations will start emitting to the log file again. 

cc @cjcenizal
comments:
Makes sense to me! Thanks for catching this Jake.

> As a result, a deprecation message is only emitted to the log the first time it is encountered after a fresh start.

I have to admit this isn't the behavior I've observed. When I tested out this feature on a 7.16 Cloud deployment, I saw numerous identical log messages being emitted.

> I saw numerous identical log messages being emitted

The same deprecation can be emitted multiple times, but we *try* to not repeat the same. The cache is 128 entries, and the key includes the xopaqueid. Is it possible the cloud deployment had a lot of deprecations and the cache was thrashing?

Minor implementation note: this issue should not be difficult to do, as we already retain the filter we add to log4j, and have a reset method we expose so that the cache is reset when the deprecation index is enabled/disabled.

@rjernst FWIW I just did a different test in which I submitted numerous requests to a deprecated API on 7.16 and I was able to observe the behavior Jake described.

Could you please loop me into the work being done on this so I can verify the UX once it's merged?
Hi @cjcenizal, @pgomulka will be looking into this one in the coming days. He'll reach out so you can validate on the UX side.

review_comments:

```suggestion
            client().performRequest(new Request("DELETE", "/_cache/deprecation_log"));
```

I'm just thinking off the top of my head, no need to take seriously.
